title: Written in Pencil
angle: A pencilled date can be a genuine commitment while admitting that plans depend on conditions not yet known.
paragraphs: On a paper calendar, a date written in pencil looks different from one pressed into the page with ink. The pencilled mark is still a plan. It simply leaves visible the fact that something may change before the day arrives.

Some arrangements depend on details that are not settled yet: a repair that may take longer, a visitor’s travel, or the weather for an outdoor gathering. Calling the plan tentative does not make it meaningless. It describes its actual shape. Treating every uncertain detail as a flaw can turn ordinary coordination into a demand for guarantees nobody can honestly give.

There is a difference between keeping options open and leaving other people to guess what is happening. A clear provisional plan can say what is expected and what would change it. That is not indecision dressed up as flexibility; it is a more accurate account of the situation. Certainty may feel reassuring, but it is not the only sign of care or seriousness. Sometimes the honest mark is the one that can still be read after an eraser has been used.
